source: Flavell (1979) Metacognition and cognitive monitoring
finding: Flavell defines a four-part model of cognitive monitoring: metacognitive knowledge, metacognitive experiences, goals (tasks), and actions (strategies). Knowledge is stored world knowledge about people as thinkers, tasks and strategies.
numbers: Model with 4 classes of phenomena; knowledge has 3 variable categories: person, task, strategy.
quote: Metacognitive knowledge is that segment of your stored world knowledge that has to do with people as cognitive creatures
limits: Theory essay, not an experiment. Does not use the words declarative, procedural, conditional; those come later (Paris, Schraw).
agent_relevance: Our agent needs a stored, queryable record of person (model), task, and strategy facts, kept apart from live feelings of difficulty.

source: Flavell (1979) Metacognition and cognitive monitoring: strategy category
finding: The strategy category is knowledge of what strategies are likely to work for what subgoals and goals in what kinds of cognitive tasks. Flavell says most knowledge is an interaction of person, task and strategy.
numbers: Example given: you (unlike your brother) should use Strategy A (rather than B) in Task X (rather than Y). Three-way interaction.
quote: metacognitive knowledge actually concerns interactions or combinations among two or three of these three types of variables
limits: The interaction is an example, not tested. This is the seed of the later 'conditional knowledge' idea.
agent_relevance: Directly maps to our class record: key = (task class, operator, this model). Store it as a triple, not as a global ranking of operators.

source: Flavell (1979) Metacognition and cognitive monitoring: task category
finding: Task knowledge has two sub-parts: knowledge about the information available (abundant or meager, familiar, organised, trustworthy) and about task demands or goals (some tasks are harder even with the same information).
numbers: Example: recalling the gist of a story is easier than recalling exact wording.
limits: Only illustrative examples; no measures.
agent_relevance: Our router should read the features of the input (how much information, how trusted, what output is demanded) before picking an operator.

source: Flavell (1979) Metacognition and cognitive monitoring: person category
finding: Person knowledge splits into intra-individual differences, inter-individual differences and universals of cognition. It includes the insight that how well you know something now may not predict how well you will know it later.
numbers: Three subcategories.
limits: Pure theory.
agent_relevance: For an LLM, intra-individual means: the model's own profile on task classes. Our measured class record is that profile. Beliefs about universals (e.g. models conform to a stated answer) are the guardrails.

source: Flavell (1979) Metacognition and cognitive monitoring: failure modes of knowledge
finding: Flavell warns that metacognitive knowledge can be inaccurate, can fail to be activated when needed, can fail to influence behaviour, and can fail to help even when it does.
numbers: Four distinct failure modes listed.
quote: it can be inaccurate, can fail to be activated when needed, can fail to have much or any influence when activated
limits: Stated as belief, not measured.
agent_relevance: Gives a failure taxonomy for the agent: wrong record, record not retrieved, retrieved but ignored, used but unhelpful. Each can be logged separately.

source: Flavell, Friedrichs & Hoyt (1970) study as reported in Flavell (1979)
finding: Founding paradigm. Children studied items until sure they could recall them perfectly. Older children said ready and usually were (perfect recall). Younger children said ready and usually were not.
numbers: Preschool and elementary children; exact N and recall rates are not given in the 1979 essay.
quote: The younger children studied for a while, said they were ready, and usually were not.
limits: Numbers are in the 1970 paper, not opened. Developmental result, not an adult strategy-selection result.
agent_relevance: Shows that a feeling of readiness without a check is unreliable. Matches G3 and G6: do not trust self-report of being done, check on something held out.

source: Markman (1977) study as reported in Flavell (1979)
finding: Children asked to help judge the adequacy of instructions that were riddled with blatant omissions. Younger children were poor at detecting them and wrongly thought they understood.
numbers: Elementary school children; exact figures are in Markman (1977), not opened.
limits: Comprehension monitoring, which is a regulation measure more than knowledge.
agent_relevance: Same lesson for LLMs: a model will feel it understood a flawed prompt. Detection needs an outside signal.

source: Schraw & Dennison (1994) Assessing metacognitive awareness (Metacognitive Awareness Inventory)
finding: Built a 52-item self-report inventory (MAI) with eight subcomponents under two heads: knowledge of cognition (declarative, procedural, conditional) and regulation of cognition. Two experiments supported a two-factor structure.
numbers: 52 items; 8 subcomponents; two experiments, 307 undergraduates in total (from a database summary, not the paper).
quote: declarative (knowing about things), procedural (knowing about how to do things), and conditional (knowing why and when to do things)
limits: NOT opened; figures come from search summaries. The eight-factor split was not recovered cleanly by later work (see a09, a10).
agent_relevance: The three-way split (what, how, when/why) is the template for our class record: facts about operators, how to run them, and when they apply.

source: Parpala (2022) Metacognitive awareness in relation to university students' learning profiles (uses a shortened MAI-style scale)
finding: Used 18 awareness items. Only two dimensions emerged (knowledge about cognition, regulation of cognition), not eight. Knowledge about cognition scored higher than regulation. Both related to a deep approach to learning.
numbers: N=462 third-year students. Correlation of the two dimensions r=0.497. With deep approach r=0.527 (knowledge) and 0.552 (regulation). Unreflective approach: -0.541 and -0.223. CFA: CFI 0.92, TLI 0.89, RMSEA 0.077.
limits: Self-report only. Three-way declarative/procedural/conditional split not recovered. Author notes remaining challenges in MAI factor structure.
agent_relevance: The three kinds of knowledge may not be separable as measured traits in humans. For our agent, split them by data type (fact, procedure, condition) not by hoping for separate faculties.

source: Harrison & Vallin (2018) Evaluating the MAI using empirical factor-structure evidence
finding: Iterative factor analysis kept a 19-item version with two factors (knowledge of cognition, regulation of cognition) and good fit in US undergraduates. Secondary reports say several earlier attempts failed to recover the original eight-factor model.
numbers: 19 items retained, 2 factors (as reported by a citing paper, not the original).
limits: NOT opened. Details taken from search summaries of citing work. DOI not verified.
agent_relevance: Do not build the schema on the claim that three separate knowledge types are empirically distinct in people. Use them as design vocabulary only.

source: Didolkar et al. (2024) Metacognitive Capabilities of LLMs: math problem solving
finding: Asked GPT-4-0613 to name the skill needed for each training question, then cluster to coarse skills. At test time the model picks a skill label from the list and gets exemplars tagged with that skill. This tests an LLM's declarative-plus-conditional knowledge: which skill fits which problem.
numbers: GSM8K: about 500 raw skill names clustered to 22. MATH: about 5,000 raw names clustered to 117. 7,000 GSM8K and 7,500 MATH training items labelled.
limits: Skill labels are the model's own; no human check of each label beyond examples. Llama-2 70B could not produce sensible labels.
agent_relevance: Direct precedent for a class record keyed by LLM-named skill classes. Granularity matters: too fine overfits, too coarse loses signal.

source: Didolkar et al. (2024): MATH text results
finding: Skill-matched exemplars beat topic-matched exemplars and beat complex-CoT on MATH with GPT-4-0613.
numbers: MATH overall: CoT 42.2, Complex CoT 50.30, CoT+Topic 50.31, CoT+Skill 53.88. Gain over CoT is 11.6 points. Geometry 41.75 vs 39.45 topic; Precalculus 33.70 vs 31.13.
limits: Single model family, single run, no confidence intervals.
agent_relevance: Choosing demonstrations by predicted skill class beat choosing by broad topic. Supports routing by fine class rather than by domain.

source: Didolkar et al. (2024): GSM8K and code results
finding: Gains are smaller where the baseline is strong. Skill selection also helps program-aided prompts.
numbers: GSM8K GPT-4: CoT 93.00, CoT+Random 92.87, CoT+Skill 94.31, with maj@5 95.38. GPT-3.5: Retrieval-RSD 76.8, Skill 82.03. MATH PAL 4-shot 52.0 -> 59.32 (3 skill + 1 code) -> 62.00 (7 skill + 1 code).
limits: Random exemplars from the same repository did not help (92.87 vs 93.00), so the gain comes from the match, not from the repository.
agent_relevance: A strong control: random-from-same-pool equals baseline. Our class record needs the same control (random operator at equal tokens).

source: Didolkar et al. (2024): transfer across models and datasets
finding: Labels made by GPT-4 helped a weaker model (Mixtral 8x7B), and GSM8K skills transferred to six other word-problem sets. Mixtral could not cluster skills (put all in one cluster).
numbers: Mixtral MATH: CoT maj@4 28.4; Skill maj@4 32.44; Topic maj@4 30.75; without SC Skill 28.44 vs Topic 26.14. Transfer to SVAMP, ASDiv, SingleOP, SingleEQ, AddSub, MultiArith: skill best in 4 of 6 cases vs CoT+PAL.
limits: Making the skill map needs a strong model; using it works for weaker models. Pre-clustering labels were used for transfer because clustered ones were too coarse.
agent_relevance: The class record can be built once by a strong model and used by cheaper ones. Building it is the hard part.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Self-Discover
finding: The model selects from 39 seed reasoning modules (critical thinking, step-by-step, etc.), adapts them to the task, and implements them as a JSON reasoning structure once per task. Then each instance follows that structure. This is task-level procedural-conditional knowledge.
numbers: BBH (23 tasks): PaLM 2-L direct 56, CoT 60, Plan-and-Solve 61, Self-Discover 67. GPT-4: 58, 75, 73, 81. T4D: PaLM 2-L 30/40/42/69, GPT-4 51/52/53/85. MATH: PaLM 2-L 45/42/49/50.5; GPT-4 70.5/71/70/73.
limits: Gain on MATH is small (1 to 7 points PaLM 2-L, 2 to 3 GPT-4). 74.7% of MATH failures are arithmetic execution errors, not structure errors. Best on world-knowledge tasks.
agent_relevance: Selecting a strategy once per task class is cheap and helps most where the task needs a non-default framing. It does not fix execution errors, so keep code-checked steps (G2, G3).

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Self-Discover: efficiency and structure quality
finding: Per-task structure discovery needs only a few extra calls at the task level, so it beats heavy sampling at a fraction of the compute.
numbers: Claimed 10-40x less inference compute than CoT-self-consistency while more than 20% better on some tasks; beats direct on 23/25 tasks and CoT on 21/25 tasks (PaLM 2-L); structures judged correct 87.5% of the time on a MATH error sample.
limits: Compute claim compared with many-sample self-consistency on selected tasks. Structures judged by human experts on a small sample.
agent_relevance: Supports G7 (pay for itself): a per-class selection step is amortised over all instances of the class.

source: Wang & Zhao (2024) Metacognitive Prompting Improves Understanding in LLMs
finding: A five-stage prompt (understand, judge, evaluate, decide, assess confidence) mirrors introspective steps. It helped across ten language-understanding datasets and four models, but it is a fixed prompt, not selected per task.
numbers: Zero-shot GPT-4 on one dataset: CoT 88.9/84.7, PS 89.4/85.3, MP 89.9/86.2; another: CoT 54.7/38.5, PS 58.3/41.7, MP 64.0/45.3. Reported gains over PS of 4.3 (MedNLI), 9.6 (UNFAIR-ToS), 12.4 (EUR-LEX).
limits: Gains are modest on most sets (about 1 to 2 points). Single-run tables, no variance. Human metacognition used as inspiration, not as a tested mechanism.
agent_relevance: A fixed 'think about what you know' prompt gives small gains. It does not test strategy selection. Treat as weak support, and note G1 (no forced doubt on a schedule).

source: Chen et al. (2026) Metacognition-as-Reward (MaR)
finding: Uses the Schraw/Dennison split as a training signal. Model rollouts are scaffolded into a metacognitive knowledge part (task-relevant information) and a regulation part (plan and adjust). Reward covers knowledge coverage, regulation fidelity and answer correctness.
numbers: Qwen3.5-9B: base 66.7 average, DAPO 65.0, MaR 67.6 on 10 science and medical benchmarks; best gains +7.7 over base and +11.0 over DAPO; Qwen3.5-4B improved on 9 of 10 (GPQA-Diamond +5.4). OOD: knowledge score up 17.2 on average, regulation 10.7, correctness 9.8. About 32K training samples; judge Qwen3.5-397B.
limits: Trains weights, which our scaffold forbids. Reward parts are scored by an LLM judge, so may inherit judge bias. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Evidence that an explicit 'knowledge of what the task needs' step can be worth having. For us it supports a task-knowledge slot before the attempt, filled by code or retrieval.

source: Didolkar et al. (2025) Metacognitive Reuse
finding: The model reflects on its own traces and writes 'behaviors' (name plus instruction) such as inclusion-exclusion or estimate-reasonableness. A handbook of behaviors is retrieved by topic at inference. This is procedural knowledge stored as named recipes.
numbers: Behavior-conditioned inference cuts reasoning tokens by up to 46% at matched or better accuracy on MATH-500 and AIME-24/25. Behavior-guided self-improvement gets up to 10% higher accuracy than critique-and-revise. Handbook from 1k MATH training questions; accuracy averaged over 5 seeds (MATH), 80 runs (AIME).
limits: Retrieval is by topic matching, not dynamic during long solutions (authors list this as a limitation). Math only. Maximum gains, not averages.
agent_relevance: Closest published analogue of a class record that stores how-to knowledge per class. Also shows storing procedures reduces tokens, which counts under G7.

source: Zhuang et al. (2026) Metacognitive Consolidation (MC2)
finding: Splits solving into reasoner, monitor and controller roles and consolidates lessons across instances into reusable procedural meta-knowledge, which grows with experience.
numbers: GPT-4o-mini MATH-500 78.93 -> 85.13; TheoremQA 46.92 -> 55.96; Game-of-24 41.33 -> 88.67; Llama-3.1-8B MATH-500 65.47 -> 76.80; Gemini-2.0-flash 94.93 -> 96.73. Tokens on MATH-500 1631 vs CoT-SC 3200 and ToT 3473. Ablation (MATH-500): Reasoner only 72.67, with updates 80.47, full 85.13. Three seeds, 95% CIs.
limits: Preprint. Accuracy improves over iterations on the same distribution; benefit larger for weaker backbones, small on GSM8K. Instance order matters (tested in appendix).
agent_relevance: Accumulating a per-class record across instances beat episodic meta-reasoning at lower token cost. Fits our design of a persistent class record with updates.

source: Wang (2026) MIRROR benchmark of metacognitive calibration
finding: Tests whether LLMs use self-knowledge to choose actions (the conditional-knowledge test). Models showed above-chance domain-level self-knowledge but failed to act on it: giving them their own calibration scores did not reduce failures; removing the decision from the model did.
numbers: 16 models, 8 labs, about 250,000 instances. Confident failure rate: C1 0.600, C2 (told own calibration) 0.605, C3 (normative instruction) 0.514, C4 (external control) 0.143, a 76% cut (45.7 points). C1->C2 p=0.90; C2->C3 p=0.0004; C3->C4 p<0.0001. MIRROR gap mean 0.170 (overconfidence). Natural accuracy 0.235 to 0.499.
limits: Single-author independent preprint. C4 assumes escalated tasks are resolved by an oracle; with a fallible resolver (50.2% correct) system success rises 0.373 -> 0.475 (+10.2 points). 20-person human pilot was at ceiling.
agent_relevance: Strong support for 'code decides': the model can know its weak domains yet does not act on it. Our class record should be applied by the program, not offered to the model as advice.

source: Wang (2026) MIRROR: transfer and composition of self-knowledge
finding: Self-knowledge is domain-specific. Calibration in one domain barely carries to others, and models cannot predict performance on tasks that combine domains.
numbers: Transfer Influence Index 0.019 to 0.175 across 11 models. Compositional Calibration Error 0.500 to 0.943 (15 models, v1) and 0.434 to 0.758 (16 models, v2); balanced v2 mean 0.529.
limits: Benchmark is new and not independently replicated. Preprint.
agent_relevance: A class record cannot be assumed to generalise across classes or to mixed-class tasks. Measure per class, and treat mixed tasks as unknown.

source: Cao et al. (2026) LLMs Know When They Know, but Do Not Act on It
finding: A harness elicits a pre-solve feeling of knowing (FOK) and post-solve judgment of learning (JOL) from the model, then code uses them to decide when to stop, retry or aggregate. This is monitoring used as control, on Claude Sonnet-4.6.
numbers: Pooled accuracy 48.3 -> 56.9. By first-attempt confidence: low 0.16 -> 0.42; medium 0.36 -> 0.55; high 0.67 -> 0.64 (no gain). Ablation on 100 items (Pass@1 44.0, Oracle@4 53.0): full 47.0, JOL-only 45.0, FOK-only 42.0, random retry at matched K 45.7, full previous reasoning context 40.0. AUROC FOK 0.534 to 0.818, JOL 0.655 to 0.745 by benchmark.
limits: Random retry at matched budget is inside the confidence interval of the full system (45.7 [43,48] vs 47.0 [37,57]); a reviewer noted missing signal-agnostic controls. FOK AUROC 0.534 on one benchmark is near chance.
agent_relevance: Confidence signals are usable but weak, and gains come mostly on items the model flags as hard. Matches G1: act on a signal. Also warns that keeping full prior context anchors on failure (40.0).

source: Khandelwal et al. (2025) SOFAI-LM: LLMs coupled with metacognition
finding: A metacognitive module monitors a fast LLM, feeds back concrete errors and examples, and calls a slow reasoning model only when the loop fails. This is strategy selection (fast or slow solver) by a code-side controller.
numbers: Code debugging: SOFAI-LM solves Python 70% and C++ 73% vs LRM alone 37% (Python) and 40% (C++), in less time. Graph coloring (Granite 3.3 8B fast, DeepSeek R1 8B slow): about 42% with memory-augmented feedback; LRM alone solves 2% in one panel.
limits: Small open models (8B). Two task families. Time reported, not matched tokens.
agent_relevance: A routing rule (fast first, escalate on repeated failure) can beat always using the heavy solver. A code-side escalation rule is the conditional-knowledge use we want.

source: Luo et al. (2025) Learning from Peers in Reasoning Models (prefix dominance trap)
finding: Starting a reasoning model with the first 15% of tokens from a wrong response cuts accuracy by about 20%; the models rarely recover. This is the cost of committing to a poor early path without monitoring.
numbers: Prefix = first 15% of tokens from incorrect responses; 16 continuations per prefix at temperature 1; about 20% accuracy loss. LeaP gives QwQ-32B nearly 5 points on the tested benchmarks (AIME 2024/2025, AIMO 2025, GPQA Diamond).
limits: Tested on reasoning models and hard math; not a test of strategy knowledge itself. Cited by MGV as motivation.
agent_relevance: Argues for choosing the approach before generating, and for the program (not the model) to reset when a start looks bad. Supports a pre-attempt operator choice.

source: Oh & Gobet (2025) Monitor-Generate-Verify (MGV)
finding: Translates Flavell's model into algorithms: monitoring (difficulty, confidence, strategy retrieval) happens before generation, and verification feedback updates the monitoring knowledge. It notes Flavell has no explicit working-memory mechanism.
numbers: No experiments. Cites a roughly 20% accuracy loss from the prefix dominance trap (Luo et al. 2025) as motivation. Links to resource-rational models (Callaway et al. 2022, 2024).
limits: Authors state they present no empirical validation. Conceptual only.
agent_relevance: Gives a precise vocabulary: knowledge base updated from verification, experiences as triggers. Our class record plus impasse detector map onto it. Needs testing before any claim.

source: Schraw & Moshman (1995) Metacognitive theories
finding: Reviews metacognitive theories; distinguishes tacit, informal and formal theories of cognition and separates knowledge of cognition from regulation. Described in secondary sources as the source of the three-way declarative/procedural/conditional split used in the MAI.
numbers: No numbers collected; full text not available this session.
limits: NOT opened. Attempts to fetch a free copy failed (HTTP 403 / HTML page returned). Content description is from background knowledge.
agent_relevance: Historical anchor only. Cite only after reading.

source: Paris, Lipson & Wixson (1983) Becoming a strategic reader
finding: Origin of the declarative, procedural and conditional division of strategy knowledge in reading instruction: knowing that, knowing how, knowing when and why. Conditional knowledge was argued to be the part most often missing.
numbers: No numbers collected; not opened.
limits: NOT opened. Content is from background knowledge and secondary summaries, treat as unverified.
agent_relevance: The 'when and why' part is what our class record is for. Verify against the paper before relying on any claim.
